t: Smallest Value After Replacing With Sum of Prime Factors — Simulation
o: Repeatedly replace n by the sum of its prime factors with multiplicity until the value stops changing (which happens exactly at primes and at n=4, since 4 → 2+2+2... wait, 4 → 2+2 = 4, a fixed point). Trial division factorization per step is O(√n); the sequence shrinks quickly, so total work is tiny for n <= 1e5. Example: 15 → 3+5=8 → 2+2+2=6 → 2+3=5 (prime, stop) → 5.
k: Iterate f(n)=sum of prime factors with multiplicity until fixed point; fixed points are primes and 4.
Trial division up to sqrt(n) per step; the sequence decreases fast so few iterations occur.
Track the minimum value seen across the whole trajectory (values can dip non-monotonically? they never increase past the start, but taking min during iteration is safest).

a.i: Write a helper spf-sum that trial-divides by d=2,3,... and accumulates divisors with multiplicity (leftover >1 adds itself). Loop: compute next = f(cur); stop when next == cur; keep the minimum seen. Since f(n) <= n with equality only at primes and 4, termination is guaranteed within a handful of steps.
s: Compute s = sum of prime factors of cur with multiplicity.
If s == cur, return best (fixed point); else cur = s, best = min(best, cur), repeat.
a.t: O(√n · steps) — each factorization is O(√n); the trajectory length is very small in practice (bounded roughly by log n).

w: Fixed-point subtlety: 4 = 2+2 maps to itself, and primes map to themselves — the loop condition handles both. Don't forget the leftover factor > 1 after trial division. A sieve of smallest prime factors could speed factorization to O(log n) per query if there were many queries; unnecessary here. Follow-up: prove the trajectory always terminates and bound its length.
